entries.subject: shortening generalises past the walk: four seconds keeps the face on 3 of 4, seven on 1 of 4
entries.body:
The four-second result was proven on a walk toward the camera, the motion that fails hardest,
and the advice the studio now gives on every motion rested on a survival number rather than a
trial. The takes on the box could not check it - almost none are under four and a half
seconds, because four second shots are a thing the studio only started asking for this
afternoon. So the same still medium shot, same place, same person, same words, was built at
two lengths with four seeds each:

  four seconds    3 of 4 kept the face
  seven seconds   1 of 4 kept it

Same engine, same anchor, same everything but the number in the length field. The one failure
at four seconds started from a composed face of 0.45 where its siblings started near 0.67 -
the other law showing through, that a shot which begins badly does not recover.

entries.author: sechang11
entries.subject: a head too small to read is not a different face
entries.body:
Rendered on purpose, because no amount of looking at existing takes could answer it: the
builder derives the standing distance from the framing and never varies it, so every wide
shot on the box stands at exactly the same place. The builder now takes a distance, and the
same wide shot of the same person was built at two of them, three seeds each.

  stand 0.22   head 135 px in the delivered frame   the face scores 0.655, 0.66, 0.675
  stand 0.62   head  65 px                          the same face scores 0.27, 0.30, 0.30, 0.32

That is not a degraded face. It is an unreadable one, and the ruler was calling it "a
different face" - which is a fault, which sends Make to render the shot again on another seed.
A seed cannot make a head bigger. Below a hundred pixels of head the ruler now says it cannot
judge, and the studio stops re-rolling shots for a failure that is geometry.

It also explains the framing table cleanly: a close-up keeps the face on 17 of 19 takes and a
full-length framing on 1 of 6, and it is head pixels all the way down.

entries.subject: 45 of 45 entries built and measured, and a shot now records which entry built it
entries.body:
The catalog promises that every entry has been built once and measured, and the shelf shows
the result. That record was written by the matrix driver, and a shot built straight from the
builder carried no trace of which entry it came from - so the thirteen entries added today
read as never built when ten of them already had been. A shot now stores its template, the
ten got their record from the film they were built into, and the last three (matched angles,
crane down onto a face, four seconds and the face holds) were built to close the set.

Also: the angle log said "asked +0.32, the plate measures +0.32 (eye level)", which is two
true halves making a sentence that denies its own success - the arithmetic landed exactly and
+0.32 is inside what ordinary photographs do, now that the words come from the population. It
reports the CHANGE from the source plate instead.

entries.author: sechang11
entries.subject: who loses the face: three laws from 119 clocked takes, and one idea that did not survive them
entries.body:
by framing        close 17 of 19 kept the face (89%)   wide 33 of 50 (66%)   full 1 of 6 (17%)
  by the place      held 42 of 52 (81%)   drifted 20 of 37 (54%)   changed 0 of 5 (0%)
  by the first frame  0.65+ 45 of 62 (73%)   0.55-0.65 31 of 40 (78%)   under 0.55 4 of 17 (24%)

The place and the face fail together, and completely: on the five takes whose place changed
between the first frame and the last, not one kept the face. An engine that rewrites the
scene rewrites the person in it. And a bigger head survives - a close-up holds the face nine
times in ten where a full-length framing holds it once in six.

The third row looked like a chance to catch a failure before spending any card time, since
the anchor is a still picture that exists before the render. It does not work. Measured on 65
shots that have both, the anchor and the take's first frame are not the same measurement: the
take reads 0.069 higher at the median with a spread of 0.103, because one is a plate-sized
composite and the other is the engine's rendering of it at the film's resolution. Across that
offset the anchor separates 67 per cent from 79. Real, and smaller than the noise it would be
read through. So identity.py can now score a still, the compositor records what the anchor
scored, and nothing is gated on it - a 67-against-79 predictor would throw away good anchors
and keep bad ones while looking rigorous.

entries.author: sechang11
entries.subject: the face clock advises before the render, from 101 measured takes
entries.body:
A ruler that grades a take after the fact is worth something. A ruler that changes what gets
asked for is worth much more. So the hold curve was backfilled onto every take the studio had
already made - 101 of them, on CPU, no renders - and gathered by what the shot asks the person
to do:

  still   98 takes, 68 held the face throughout, 25 lost it; three quarters held 4.8 s
  walk    17 takes, 10 held, 7 lost;                         three quarters held 4.0 s
  crouch   2 takes, neither followable - the head leaves the box the geometry predicts

The advice is a survival number, not the worst take that ever happened. The first version
spoke from the earliest moment a face had ever been lost, which let one unlucky still shot at
1.9 s cap every still shot in the studio at three seconds. It is now the length at which three
quarters of takes of that motion still held the face, with a margin so an ordinary five second
shot against a 4.8 s survival stays quiet. A warning that fires on everything is a warning
nobody reads.

The builder says it in the job log, writes it into the spec, and the length field on the page
says it live as the director types. A motion the ruler cannot follow says nothing rather than
guessing.

entries.author: sechang11
entries.subject: the angle's words come from the population, and its promise is relative to the plate
entries.body:
The ruler was calibrated against synthetic keystones, which checks that it measures what it
claims and says nothing about what the numbers should be called. The first names were picked
from theory: past 0.12 a low angle, past 0.55 a steep one. Run over every plate and picked
take on the box, 102 readings, that made two thirds of ordinary pictures "a steep low angle" -
not wrong so much as useless.

Real photographs are not shot dead level at the middle of their subject. The population's
quartiles are 0.00 and +0.80 with a median of +0.39, skewed upward because a camera held at
chest height in a street has converging verticals whether anyone asked for them or not. So
the words are set from that: the middle of the population is eye level, a low angle starts
where the top quartile does, and steep is reserved for the top tenth. Downward is rare and
gets a tighter threshold.

And because an ordinary plate is not at zero, the promise cannot be absolute. The builder
records what the source plate measured alongside what was asked, and the spec compares the
take against that plate. The same correction the keyword bench needed, and the ruler's own
calibration, and now this: score against the baseline, never against the ideal.

Also: the angle is backfilled onto every take the studio had already made, so the
encyclopedia can say where the camera stood as well as what it did. 67 takes, no renders.

entries.author: sechang11
entries.subject: a crane, and a take that survives ComfyUI being killed under it
entries.body:
The studio could put the camera below eye level or above it, but only for the whole take -
the angle lives in the plate and a plate does not move. A crane does. The same keystone the
angle pass applies to a plate, applied per frame with a pitch that ramps, inside a zoom that
gives it room so no pixel outside the frame is ever asked for. Measured at the first frame
and the last: direction correct on four of four, and asked -0.70 from a plate at +0.40
delivered -0.76. What it cannot do is the parallax, because the depth map belongs to the
plate and a rendered take has no depth per frame - so it is a boom on a locked head, and the
entry says so.

And the box killed ComfyUI twice in an hour while staging a 20 GB video model, because
another session was holding the card. No exception, no traceback, the socket simply closes -
the signature already written down for oversized renders. The studio knew how to bring it
back and was not calling that where it mattered: a submission into a closed socket raised
straight out of the take and the variant was recorded as failed. Six submission sites now
bring ComfyUI back and try once more. Once, not forever - if the box genuinely cannot fit
the model then retrying is a loop and the honest failure is the one to report.

entries.author: sechang11
entries.subject: a pack view can be drawn out of proportion, and eight of eighteen packs have one
entries.body:
Every composite scales a cutout so its total height is what a 1.7 m person subtends where it
stands. That only holds together if all the views of one person share proportions, and
measured across the packs on this box they do not: the well-behaved ones vary 13 to 33 per
cent in head size between views of the same character, and eight packs have at least one view
more than a third away from their own median - a hat brim, a raised arm, a failed cutout or a
figure that is not standing. Those views are in active use, and a wide composed from one and a
medium composed from another give the same person two different head sizes.

_tools/pack_views_check.py names them, per pack, with the view to re-render, and the repair
job now removes those as well as the ones the truncation detector calls cropped. compose gains
head_frac() and head_reference(), the pack's own median over its turnaround, cached beside it.

Scaling by the head was tried and withdrawn in the same hour, honestly: it did not reach the
path that composes the subject, and measuring a head in a finished composite is not the same
measurement as measuring one in a clean cutout - the relight changes the silhouette's top
rows and the numbers did not track the source proportions. Changing how every anchor in the
studio is sized on the strength of a measurement that shaky would be the opposite of
precision. The diagnostic is where the value was.

Also learned the hard way: a hundred segmenter calls back to back killed ComfyUI while another
session held the GPU - no exception, the socket simply closes, the signature already written
down for big renders. The check is paced now.

entries.author: sechang11
entries.subject: a whole low view for the packs, and what the retry sentence was quietly costing
entries.body:
A low angle on the place was arithmetic; a low angle on the PERSON needs a picture of the
person from below, and the pack's own pres_low is cropped at the knees in every pack on the
box - correct for a presentation card, useless for compositing, which needs feet to stand a
figure on ground. So the packs gain pres_low_full, made through the same must-be-whole
renderer, and the builder uses it when the angle is a low one and says plainly when a pack
has none.

The first four came back whole and three of them were not low angles at all. The cause is
the renderer's fallback: when a figure runs off the bottom of the frame it adds a FAR
FRAMING sentence, and standing well back moves the camera to eye level. One pack came back
crouching. The detector was satisfied every time because the detector measures wholeness and
nothing else. The law: a retry sentence must restate what the shot must not lose. The retry
here names the framing AND the angle AND the pose, and when it is still cropped it extends
the picture downward rather than surrendering the angle.

Both gates now apply, because either alone is fooled: the truncation detector for wholeness,
and the silhouette's bottom-heaviness against the pack's own eye-level full body for the
angle. A view that is whole but at eye level is worse than no view - the builder would use
it for a low angle and the picture would quietly disagree with the promise - so a pack that
fails loses the file. Two of four kept: tomas-reyl at +0.142, mara-okonjo at +0.078.

Also measured: extending the picture downward dilutes the second ruler, because the legs it
adds are not foreshortened. The ruler is honest about a render and not about an outpaint.

entries.subject: the angle, measured and then performed: a low angle is arithmetic on the plate
entries.body:
Two new tools and a correction to the pick.

anglemeasure.py says where the camera IS, as cammeasure says what it did. A camera tilted
up makes the world's verticals converge toward the top of the frame, so: Canny, Hough,
keep the near-vertical segments, and find the point most of them agree on. RANSAC, not
least squares - least squares was the first attempt and it failed on the one answer that
matters most, calling a picture of parallel verticals a steep angle because a few outliers
pulled the fit. Calibrated against synthetic keystones of a known pitch: median error 0.008
and worst 0.045 on seven of eight plates. The eighth is a harbour reverse whose masts and
rigging are not a vertical family; there the ruler says so and promises nothing.

angle.py performs it. A low angle is two things that must happen together: the camera drops
(near things fall in the frame more than far things - parallax, from the depth map) and the
camera tilts up (verticals converge, and the view rises). Doing only the second measures
right and looks like a lens fault. The framing move runs inside a zoom, the way postmove
does a tilt, so no pixel outside the plate is ever invented. Delivered pitch against asked:
exact to 0.02 on every place the ruler can read. angled_plate() keeps the result beside its
plate with a warped depth map, so compose, the footing check, the identity head box and the
spec all treat it as what it is - the same place, from a different camera. The pickers hide
derived plates.

And the pick was rewarding a repair. The first build with the face-cut on came back with one
take that ran the full six seconds and kept the face, and one that lost the face at three
seconds and was cut to three - and the cut one won, on a camera reading a hair closer to the
static that was asked. Three seconds of the right shot is not better than six. What the take
delivers against what the shot asked now sorts above how exactly the camera matched.

spec all treat it as what it is - the same place, from a different camera. The pickers hide
derived plates.

And the pick was rewarding a repair. The first build with the face-cut on came back with one
take that ran the full six seconds and kept the face, and one that lost the face at three
seconds and was cut to three - and the cut one won, on a camera reading a hair closer to the
static that was asked. Three seconds of the right shot is not better than six. What the take
delivers against what the shot asked now sorts above how exactly the camera matched.

entries.subject: the face has a clock: identity measured over time, the take cut where the face goes
entries.body:
Measured on 51 picked takes: the face does not fail at the end, it decays through the clip.
Median score as a fraction of its own start: 1.00 at the top, 0.977 at a quarter, 0.962 at
half, 0.911 at three quarters, 0.886 at the end - most of the loss in the last quarter. On a
walk toward the camera the crossing has a clock: 3.7 s, 4.5 s and 4.5 s of six second takes.

identity.py now scores nine points through a clip with the head box carried through the
camera as measured AT THAT TIME (cammeasure's per-step curve), and reports holds_until and
lost_at in seconds. The camera pass keeps its curve on the take so this can be re-scored
without a render. The note says "the face holds for the first 4.5 s of 6.0". The pick
prefers the take whose face lasts longest. A shot with cam.trim_face asks the studio to cut
the take at that moment: never below two seconds, and the cut take is no longer faulted for
a face it no longer contains.

match the 2.5 int8 model by name and it does change the picture (the same seed rendered a
13% push instead of a static), but it does not hold the face - lost at 4.53 s against the
control's 4.47, end 0.30 against 0.30. Kept as workflows/70_ltx25_i2v_lora.json for the next
LoRA to be tried through, not adopted.

entries.author: sechang11
entries.subject: pin: the end figure keeps the start figure's feet and scale
entries.body:
qwen-edit regenerates composition as well as content. Asked for a crouch
with "same camera, same framing", it returned the crouch a quarter nearer
the camera (head 76 px vs 61); asked for "walked closer", it returned a
medium shot, four times the size. H3 interpolated what it was given: a
walk-forward before the crouch, and an invented landscape sliding past
the walker.

The compositor knows the start figure's geometry from the anchor recipe,
so the end figure is now constrained rather than asked for. In-place
motions (crouch, rise, turn, look, reach, gesture, nod): feet on the start
figure's ground line, same centre, scaled so the head is as wide as the
start figure's - head width being the one measure a pose leaves alone.
Moving motions (walk, run): scale change clamped to 0.6-1.6x and the feet
placed where the plate's own depth puts a figure of that height. The start
silhouette is recovered as the difference between the start frame and the
pristine plate. `hold_feet` chooses; the editor has a "feet planted" box
that the motion selector sets. The plate floor moves to 0.002 (the held
crouch measures 0.0028-0.0032/s) and a subject-region change is logged for
the next calibration.

entries.subject: film: a resolution target per film, and a per-shot triage of local vs API
entries.body:
Resolution was derived, silently: the compiler took the largest megapixel
count the shot's length permitted, so an 8s shot came out near 1080p and
a 30s shot at 720p and nothing said that shortening would sharpen. Films
now carry a target (auto / 720p / 1080p / max). The compiler honours it
where the envelope allows and otherwise renders what fits and warns with
the exact cut that would recover the target.

Triage answers "what do we make here and what needs API help" from the
measured envelope, per shot, with reasons in words: over 30s in one shot,
more than two identities in a frame, a camera move on LTX (advisory), a
multi-beat character shot without a composed anchor, anime dialogue (no
lip sync). Verdicts are local / trade-off / api; the review tab shows them.

A deliver (upscale) field exists on the film but is withdrawn from the UI
until an upscaler is wired to master.

entries.body:
Everything the last stretch produced - compose, depth placement, pinning, the
camera and motion vocabularies - was reachable only by typing python over ssh,
which is the opposite of "select for each field".

  POST /api/film/compose   pick a character and a place, get a still with the
                           character IN it, set as that shot's anchor. Verified
                           by clicking: plate fidelity L=0.0003 R=0.0000, and
                           the shot comes back with anchor_source recorded.
  POST /api/film/pin       say what changes; the end state is an edit of the
                           shot's own anchor and H3 interpolates. Refuses when
                           the pin rate is too low rather than rendering
                           invention.
  GET  /api/film/foundry_assets  what the foundry holds, so the pickers list
                           real assets instead of asking anyone to remember ids.

the dictionary, so camera and motion were invisible purely because two loops
said ["character","place","costume","prop","music"]. The list now comes from

anchor - including the bare plate that produced a different woman after the cut,
which is the exact case the warning exists for. `file:` means "a specific
image", not "an image with the character in it". It now keys on anchor_source,

entries.subject: playbook 21-24: the compositor, depth placement, motion, and scoping one-beat
entries.body:
The operating guide knew nothing about the last stretch of work - zero mentions
of compose, pinned, advisory or depth - which makes it a guide to a system that
no longer exists. Four sections, written from measurements rather than intent:

  21  the compositor. Why it is five steps and not one prompt (a "relit"
      composite sat 0.187 from its own plate, against 0.211 for a different time
      of day - the model regenerates rather than edits), why the guard is
      proportion and not edges, and the backwards intuition that cost two runs:
      a BIGGER figure on the relight canvas drifts less, 16% against 30-37%.

  22  ground placement from depth. One dial sets position and scale together, so
      a figure can no longer be far away and gigantic. The horizon is where the
      ground stops receding, not where depth is greatest - the first detector
      took the sky and returned its own floor as an answer. And what depth still
      does not know: whether the ground is standable.

  23  motion. Requested is advisory, pinned is real. Three suspects for why
      prose cannot direct LTX - the enhancer, the wording, the position - all
      three isolated and all three wrong; it is an engine prior. Pinning both
      ends is deterministic, and needs enough change PER SECOND, not enough
      change: the same pin fails at 8s and works at 3.75s.

  24  the one-beat rule was measuring the anchor. It holds for plate anchors and
      does not apply to composited ones, so multi-beat shots are safe when the
      character is in the start frame. Also states what was NOT established -
      whether LTX rendered an actual hard cut - because the frame-delta detector
      scores a known-good multishot lower than the clip under test, which means
      the metric is wrong rather than the courier.

Every section carries the numbers and, where a guess was wrong, the wrong guess.
The guide is most useful where it says what does not work.

entries.subject: one-beat doctrine: it was measuring the anchor, not the cut
entries.body:
THE DOCTRINE, as film.py warns: "an internal cut re-derives faces from the scene
prior - the start frame's face does not survive it. For identity-critical
moments use ONE-beat shots from identity keyframes and cut at assembly instead."
It cost THE LANTERN THIEF nineteen renders where five or six would have done.

It was established when anchors were scene plates. We now know a scene plate
does not put the character in the frame at all, so the doctrine may never have
been about cuts.

Two arms, same two beats, same prompt, differing only in the first frame:

  composite  she is physically in the plate before LTX runs
             -> the same woman throughout. Medium in the first half, close-up in
                the second, and it is Mara in both: same face, same single
                braid, same freckles, same jacket.
  plate      the bare plate, character in words - how the editor works today
             -> the first half is an empty street with one distant figure, and
                the close-up after the transition is a DIFFERENT WOMAN. Box
                braids instead of a single braid, a different face entirely.

So the doctrine holds for plate anchors and does not apply to composited ones.
Multi-beat shots are safe when the character is in the start frame, which means
the shot count of a film like THE LANTERN THIEF is roughly a third of what the
one-beat rule forced.

WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED, and is stated rather than glossed: whether LTX rendered
an actual hard cut. A frame-delta detector at 8fps gives 3.3x for this clip
against 1.7x for THE COURIER, a multishot previously accepted as having real
cuts - so the detector cannot separate a cut from a fast push at that sampling
rate, and a lower score on a known-good clip means it is the metric that is
wrong, not the courier. The identity conclusion does not depend on it: the
post-transition face is either the same person or a different one, and that is
directly visible.

Both clips are at /verify/motion under one sentence.
